The hatchling emerges from the calcareous egg after an incubation period of 19 days [ab = 19 days] when incubated at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with observed extremes of 18 to 20 days (18-20 days) [ab = 18-20 days]. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately after the chick emerges from the egg, averages 5.7 grams [Wwb = 5.7 grams]. This modest initial mass belies the rapid growth that will occur during the subsequent weeks of intense parental provisioning. The altricial nestling depends entirely on its parents for food and thermoregulation during this critical period, and the energetic demands on the provisioning adults are considerable.

The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic adult body mass, exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in the Brown cacholote. Females attain a maximum adult mass of approximately 69.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 69.3 grams], whereas males are considerably larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of about 76.5 grams [Wwi = about 76.5 grams]. This size difference is common among furnariids and is likely associated with male-male competition for nesting territories and access to mates. The larger body size of males may also confer advantages in nest construction and defense against potential predators or competitors for suitable cavities.
